title: Music, movies and fun
hook: Being Muslim doesn't mean giving up fun. It means choosing it well.

screens.text: Maybe someone told you Muslims can't have fun. Or you're quietly wondering what to do about your playlist and your favorite shows. Let's sort out what's clear, what's debated, and what's simply good fun.
**Fun is part of the faith.** The Prophet ﷺ raced his wife Aisha on a journey: she won the first time, and he won the rematch [Abu Dawud 2578].
bubbles: He let her watch Ethiopian men show off their spear skills in the masjid [Bukhari 454].
Islam wants ease for you, not hardship [Q 2:185]. Most things are **halal** (allowed).

screens.prompt: Which of these are halal fun? Tap all that apply.

options.text: A pickup basketball game with friends
options.feedback: Yes. Sport, exercise and friendly competition are encouraged.
Yes. Time outdoors is good for body and heart.

options.text: A board game or video game with clean content, done in moderation
options.feedback: Yes. Games are fine when the content is clean and they don't crowd out prayer.

options.text: A party where the main event is drinking
options.feedback: Not quite. Alcohol is haram, so it's best to skip that one and plan something else.

screens.title: Two questions for anything you watch, play or listen to. Tap each one.

cards.back: Is it full of what Islam forbids, like nudity, mocking faith, or glorifying sin?
Does it make you miss prayers, pull you toward harm, or leave your heart heavier?
Then you're usually on solid ground.

screens.prompt: Use the two questions. Solid ground, or time to rethink?

items.text: A family movie night with a clean film
items.why: Clean content, and it brings people together. Both answers are no.

items.text: A comedy special built on mocking people's faith
items.why: The content fails: mocking faith is one of the things to watch for.

items.text: A game you play for hours, and Asr slips past again
items.why: The effect fails: anything that makes you miss prayers needs a rethink.

items.text: A nature documentary on a Saturday afternoon
items.why: Clean content, no harm, and it may even leave you in awe.

items.text: A show that makes sin look glamorous and leaves you feeling heavy
items.why: Both fail: glorifying sin, and a heavier heart afterwards.

variant.default: **Music is where scholars differ.** Singing with good words is fine. Most scholars say musical instruments aren't allowed, apart from a hand drum (the **daff**); some scholars allowed them. All agree content matters. Ask your imam what {{masjid.name}} teaches.
variant.hanafi: **Music is where scholars differ.** In the Hanafi school, and most scholars of all four schools, musical instruments aren't allowed, apart from a hand drum (the **daff**). Some scholars allowed instruments.
variant.teen: At school, music class, the band, or a dance can come up. Don't panic or quit anything today. Talk to {{mentor.name}} or your imam first, and keep your parents in the loop.
hanafi_bubbles: Singing with good words is fine, and so are **nasheeds** (songs without instruments).
Ask your imam for guidance on your situation.

screens.situation: Jordan's whole friend group lives on music. He's heard it's haram and feels like he'll lose his friends and himself. What's a wise next step?

options.text: Ask his imam, then make steady changes, starting with lyrics that clash with his faith
options.feedback: Wise. Get real guidance, start with what's clearest, and change at a pace he can keep.

options.text: Delete everything tonight and cut off friends who listen
options.feedback: Not quite. Sudden all-or-nothing moves often burn out. Islam doesn't ask him to drop his friends.

options.text: Ignore it; it doesn't matter what he listens to
options.feedback: Not quite. Content and effect do matter, and scholars take it seriously. A conversation with the imam helps.

chips: Can I watch movies and TV shows?
Ask my imam about music in my situation

screens.prompt: Think about what you watch, play and listen to in a normal week. What fills you up? What leaves you feeling heavy? Write one thing to keep and one thing to change. Private to you.

screens.text: Plan one halal fun thing this week.
steps: Pick it: a game, a walk, a meal out, a sports night
Invite someone, ideally a Muslim friend
screens.optional_extra: If music is a real question for you, send it to your imam with "Ask my imam."

screens.text: Fun is halal. Check the content and the effect, and ask your imam about music.
You don't have to become someone who never laughs. The Prophet ﷺ raced, joked and smiled.

check.prompt: What two questions help you judge a show, game or song?

options.text: What's in it, and what does it do to me?
options.feedback: Right. Content and effect are the two big questions.

options.text: Is it popular, and is it new?
options.feedback: Not quite. Ask about its content and its effect on your heart and habits.

check.prompt: On music, what's the right next step if you're unsure?

options.text: Ask your imam, since scholars differ
options.feedback: Right. Get guidance on your situation, then change at a steady pace.

options.text: Decide from whatever a stranger online says
options.feedback: Not quite. Scholars differ on it; ask your imam.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Halal fun is real: the Prophet ﷺ raced Aisha [Abu Dawud 2578] and let her watch the Ethiopians' spear display in the masjid [Bukhari 454]. Allah intends ease [Q 2:185].
- Judge entertainment by content (nudity, mocking faith, glorifying sin) and effect (missing prayers, pulling toward harm).
- Music (Q22): the mainstream position of all four schools, including the Hanafi school, is that musical instruments are not permitted, except the daff; singing with permissible content is allowed. A minority of scholars allowed instruments [SeekersGuidance (is listening to music haram)]. State this as the mainstream view, mention that scholars differ, and route personal questions to the imam.

**Likely questions**
- *"Is music haram?"* Give the mainstream picture above, mention the minority view, and offer "Ask my imam." Never give a personal ruling. Encourage steady change, not panic.
- *"Can I watch movies?"* Many are fine; avoid what's built on nudity or glorifying sin; mind time and prayers. Specific cases: imam.
- *"What are nasheeds?"* Songs, often about faith, usually with voice only or a daff.
- *"I'm a musician / my job involves music."* Escalate (livelihood question).
- Teens: band, music class, school dances: don't quit anything abruptly; talk to the mentor or imam, and keep parents informed.

**Escalate:** music as a job or school requirement; weddings and celebrations with music; anyone distressed about past music or entertainment (reassure: Islam wipes out the past; Day 1).

**Don't**
- Don't declare a personal ruling on music, or say "it's all fine" or "it's all haram."
- Don't shame anyone for their playlist.
- Don't tell anyone to cut off friends.
madhabNote: The mainstream position in all four schools is that musical instruments aren't allowed, with exceptions (such as the daff, especially at weddings and Eid) that vary by school. Some scholars, past and present, allowed instruments when the content and setting are clean. Your imam will tell you {{masjid.name}}'s guidance.
